description: One reportable, actionable asset on the farm: a valve, a sprayer, a tractor, a cabin, a cold storage unit. Its durable ID tag (QR and optional NFC) lets a worker scan it, see its history, and log state changes or compliance tasks — all attached to this specific asset rather than to a location or a spreadsheet row. The docname IS the printable ID, e.g. MC-Valve-05 or HL-Sprayer-02, so a label and a record are the same string.

fields.description: What kind of asset this is. The type determines what state fields make sense (a valve is open or closed, a sprayer is full or empty) and which inspection templates apply.
fields.label: Asset Type

fields.description: The company that owns this asset.
fields.label: Company

fields.description: The parent asset for tree structure — a valve belongs to a zone, a zone belongs to a block. Any Asset Register record can be a parent, so the hierarchy is as deep or shallow as the operation needs.
fields.label: Location (Parent Asset)

fields.description: The Irrigation Zone this asset draws through, for a valve or anything below one. THE ONE LINK OUT OF THE ASSET TREE, and it exists because the tree cannot carry it: an asset's parent is another asset, so a valve could name the zone-shaped ASSET above it and never the Irrigation Zone record that holds the flow rate, the water right and the block. Without this column get_water_usage_report can count minutes and can price nothing, which is the half a water-rights filing actually asks for. Empty is fine and is the honest answer on a farm that has not mapped its zones — the report says so per valve rather than guessing a rate.
fields.label: Irrigation Zone

fields.description: What this asset is, in words. The label on the ground, the model number, whatever helps a worker standing in front of it confirm they scanned the right tag.
fields.label: Description

fields.description: When this asset was removed from service. A retired asset keeps its history and its tag but no longer appears in active lists or generates compliance alerts.
fields.label: Retired At
Capital Asset
fields.description: What an insurance schedule asks for. Empty on a valve or a cabin; filled on a tractor, an implement or a vehicle. export_insurance_schedule reads exactly these columns.

The VIN, serial number or model number stamped on the machine itself — the string an adjuster matches a claim against, and the one the iOS app captures by OCR off the plate. Not the docname: the tag ID is what this farm calls it, and this is what the manufacturer does.
fields.label: Serial / VIN

fields.description: Make and model as the manufacturer writes it, e.g. 'John Deere 5075E'. Free text rather than a link: a register of every model of every machine is a table nobody on a farm will maintain.
fields.label: Model

fields.description: When this asset was acquired. A DATE and not a datetime — nobody records the hour a tractor was bought, and a date has no timezone to get wrong.
fields.label: Date Acquired

fields.description: What was paid for it. Kept apart from replacement value for ever: an insurer settles on replacement and the books depreciate from purchase, and one column holding whichever was entered last answers neither question.
fields.label: Purchase Value

fields.description: What it would cost to replace today. This is the number an insurance schedule is written against. Where it is empty, export_insurance_schedule falls back to purchase value and SAYS it did rather than presenting a decade-old price as cover.
fields.label: Replacement Value

fields.description: The URL the QR code encodes — auto-generated from the asset name. A scanner pointed at the tag resolves here.
fields.label: QR URL

fields.description: The UID of an NFC tag physically attached to this asset. Optional — QR is the baseline transport, NFC is the fast path for assets that justify the tag cost.
fields.label: NFC UID

fields.description: Where this asset is, as a latitude. Written at registration and updated on every scan that carries a fix.
fields.label: GPS Latitude

fields.description: Where this asset is, as a longitude. Written at registration and updated on every scan that carries a fix.
fields.label: GPS Longitude

fields.description: Type-specific state as JSON — a valve's open/closed, a sprayer's full/empty, a cabin's occupied/vacant. Read and written by state-change actions (v0.25.0); stored here so a scan shows what the asset is doing right now.
fields.label: Current State

fields.description: When the state above was reached, cached from the Asset State Log row that reached it. A CACHE AND NOT A SECOND ACCOUNT: it is stamped in the same save that moves current_state, from the same timestamp the log row carries, so the two can never name different moments. Runtime is still summed from the log — this column exists so a valve list can say "open since 06:12" without one query per valve, which is what a scan screen and a dispatch board both need.
fields.label: Last State Change

fields.description: What a valve is on its line, and when it went in. Present on Asset Register rather than on a doctype of its own because a valve IS a tagged asset — it has a QR label, a state machine, a parent and a state log already, and a second table of valves would be a second account of the same pipe.
fields.label: Irrigation Valve

fields.description: Where this valve sits on the line: a Main at the turnout, a Sub-Main off it, a Lateral at the row. RANK, NOT HIERARCHY — the hierarchy is the location link above, which is what the closing cascade actually walks. This says what kind of thing a worker is standing at, and lets create_irrigation_valve refuse a Main filed underneath a Lateral, which is a data entry error the cascade would otherwise honour.
fields.label: Valve Type

fields.description: When this valve went into the ground. Separate from acquired_on, which is when it was bought — a valve sitting in the shed for a season has one date and not the other, and a line's age is what a replacement schedule is written from.
fields.label: Installed Date
Service Schedule
fields.description: When this machine is next due, and what it has run since it was last touched. Both intervals are optional and either alone is a complete schedule — a tractor is serviced on hours, a fire extinguisher on the calendar, and a pump on whichever comes first. check_maintenance_due reads exactly these columns; trigger_maintenance_tasks raises a Farm Task off them.

Hours of running between services, e.g. 250 on a tractor. Zero or empty means this machine is not on an hours schedule — which is the right answer for a valve, and is different from a schedule that is due.
fields.label: Service Interval (Hours)

fields.description: Days between services, e.g. 365 on an annual inspection. Zero or empty means this machine is not on a calendar schedule.
fields.label: Service Interval (Days)

fields.description: The date of the last completed service. The calendar interval counts from here; where it is empty and an interval is set, the asset's own creation date stands in and the answer says so.
fields.label: Last Service Date

fields.description: The hour-meter reading at the last completed service. The hours interval counts from here; where it is empty, hours since service is measured from zero.
fields.label: Hours at Last Service

fields.description: The latest hour-meter reading anybody has entered, cumulative over the life of the machine. WRITTEN BY log_asset_state_change, not typed here: a worker checking a tractor out or back in enters what the meter says and this column follows the highest reading seen. It is a CACHE of the Asset State Log's own series — get_engine_hours_summary computes every figure from the log rows, so a wrong value here cannot corrupt a season's hours.
fields.label: Current Hour Meter

fields.description: When the hour meter above was last written.
fields.label: Hours Updated At

fields.description: When this asset was last scanned by anybody.
fields.label: Last Scan At

fields.description: Who last scanned this asset.
fields.label: Last Scan By
